10C Alcohols                         
➢ Alcohols have the general formula CnH2n+1OH 
➢ The functional group is –OH.  
➢ They are good organic solvents.  
➢ They are also used as raw materials in organic synthesis.  
 
Bond angles in Alcohols 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Nomenclature 
In the IUPAC system, 
➢ Identify the longest chain of carbon atoms containing the –OH group  
➢ To show that the compound is an alcohol, suffix –e of the parent alkane is changed to -ol. 
➢ The carbon number is also added to show the location of the -OH group. 
➢ No locant is needed with only two carbons. 
➢ With longer chains, a locant is needed to tell us where on the chain the –OH group is situated.

10C Types of Alcohols 
 
➢ Alcohols are classified into different classes depending on how the –OH group is positioned 
on chain of carbon atoms.  
➢ The chemical behaviour, especially oxidation, often depends on the structural type. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Primary alcohols 
The carbon which carries the –OH group is only attached to one 
alkyl group. 
 
 
 
 
Secondary alcohols 
 
The carbon which carries the –OH group is joined directly to two 
alkyl groups. 
 
 
 
 
Tertiary alcohols 
The carbon which carries the –OH group is joined directly to three 
alkyl groups.

10C Physical properties of alcohols                       
Melting and boiling temperatures 
 
➢ Alcohols have melting and boiling temperatures much higher than those of alkanes and 
haloalkanes of comparable relative molecular mass.  
➢ This is because alcohols can form hydrogen bonding between molecules while weak 
London forces present between alkanes and dipole-dipole forces exist between 
haloalkanes.  
➢ Since hydrogen bonding is stronger, it requires more energy to break the bonds.  
 
Solubility 
➢ Alcohols with relatively short carbon chains dissolve in water.  
➢ This is because alcohols can form hydrogen bonds with water which is stronger than the 
London forces between the carbon chains of alcohols.  
➢ The solubility in water gradually decreases with increasing carbon chain length.  
➢ This is because the non-polar group of the alcohols becomes bigger which results in 
increasing the strength of London forces between carbon chains of alcohol groups.  
➢ More than one –OH groups in the molecules increases solubility since more hydrogen 
bonds can be formed between alcohol and water.

10C 3 Purifying an organic liquid                       
 
➢ Different types of reactions can be used in the preparation of organic compounds. 
➢ The organic products obtained from these reactions are not pure. It could be contaminated 
with  
• Unreacted starting materials 
• Other organic products 
• The inorganic reagents used or products formed from them 
• Water. 
Techniques used to purify the organic product 
The techniques used are based on the physical state (solid, liquid or gas) of the product. 
Common techniques include;  
• Simple distillation 
• Heat under reflux 
• Fractional distillation 
• Solvent extraction 
• Drying  
• Boiling point determination 
Distillation 
➢ Distillation is the process of separating the components or substances from a liquid mixture 
by using selective boiling and condensation. 
➢ Need to collect the distillate of the approximate boiling point range of the desired product.

Heat under reflux 
➢ Heat under reflux is used when heating organic reaction mixtures for long periods. 
➢ The condenser prevents organic vapours from escaping by condensing them back to liquids.  
 
 
 
                                                          
Fractional distillation 
Fractional distillation is the separation of a liquid 
mixture into fractions differing in boiling point by 
means of distillation, typically using a fractionating 
column. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
NOTE: Electric heaters are often used to 
heat organic chemicals. This is because 
organic chemicals are normally highly 
flammable and could set on fire with a 
naked flame. 
Anti-bumping granules are added to the flask 
in both distillation and reflux to prevent 
vigorous, uneven boiling by making small 
bubbles form instead of large bubbles. 
Never seal the end of the condenser as the build up 
of gas pressure could cause the apparatus to explode.

Separating funnel  
➢ A mixture of two immiscible liquids can be separated by using a separating funnel. 
➢ A separating funnel is a special type of funnel which has a stop-cock in its stem to allow 
the flow of a liquid from it, or to stop the flow of liquid from it. 
➢ When two immiscible liquids are placed in a separatory funnel, two layers are seen.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Drying  
➢ Final traces of water are removed by treating the organic solution with a drying agent. 
➢ A drying agent is an inorganic salt which readily takes up water to become hydrated.  
 Denser solvent will be 
the bottom layer. 
NOTE: Most halogenated 
solvents are denser than 
water, most non 
halogenated solvents are 
less dense than water. 
Solvent extraction -  Method:  
• Place reaction mixture in separating funnel and add the solvent. (it should form two 
separate layers) 
• Place stopper in the neck of the funnel and gently shake the contents, releasing 
pressure by opening the tap from time to time. 
• Allow contents to settle into two layers. 
• Remove the stopper and open the tap and collect the desired organic layer into a flask 
and discard the unwanted aqueous layer. 
 Drying an organic liquid Method:  
• Add three spatula loads of drying agent (e.g. anhydrous sodium 
sulphate, 
calcium chloride) into organic liquid. 
• Dry the organic liquid. When dry the organic liquid should appear 
clear. 
• Drying agent is removed by either decanting or filtration. 
The drying agent 
should 
•be insoluble in 
the organic liquid 
• should not 
react with the 
organic liquid.

Testing for purity - BOILING POINT DETERMINATION 
➢ Purity of liquid can be determined by measuring a boiling point.  
➢ This can be done in a distillation set up or by simply boiling a tube of the sample in an 
heating oil bath. 
➢ Once the boiling point is found the value is compared with the data booklet values and 
the purity of the compound is determined.
